clue.text: Caper around start of month to get medical treatment

indicators.note: the caper word is placed around the date, so it encloses those letters

parts.note: a caper is a playful prank or antic
SEPT I, the first of September, is the start of that month

explanation.surface: Someone takes a prank to the start of the month in order to get some medical care.
explanation.walkthrough: The month's start is a date written with a Roman numeral: Sept I, the first of September.
explanation.definitionFit: An antiseptic is a substance applied to wounds to stop infection, a basic form of medical care.

clue.text: Notice problem here at school, perhaps

parts.note: an ad is a notice in a paper
a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: A pupil spots an arithmetic problem in class.
explanation.walkthrough: Adsum is Latin for 'I am present', a traditional answer at roll call in some schools.
explanation.definitionFit: Adsum is the reply a pupil gave when their name was called on the register.

clue.text: Setter's upset — internally is melancholy

indicators.note: the little word goes inside the rearranged letters
upset means the setter word is knocked over and rearranged

parts.note: the letters of the word as written, apostrophe-s included
taken as written

explanation.surface: The puzzle setter is upset and feels sad inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s counts as a letter in the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Tristesse is a French-derived word for sadness or wistful gloom.

clue.text: What Hollywood is always after: it's somewhat charged writing above all

parts.note: film-makers are forever hunting a super script to produce
an ion is an atom carrying an electric charge

explanation.surface: Hollywood's endless quest leads to a sermon on how charged writing is the most important thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Above all' looks like emphasis but belongs to the definition: writing placed on top.
explanation.definitionFit: A superscription is an inscription or heading written over or on the outside of something.

clue.text: Dangerous rooms — no place for a king

indicators.note: the king is given no place, so his letter is removed

parts.note: parlours are sitting rooms
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: These hazardous rooms are unfit for royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Parlous is an old word meaning perilous, full of danger or uncertainty.

clue.text: Egyptian architect, I think, favoured going high

parts.note: IMHO, in my humble opinion, internet shorthand

indicators.note: in a down entry, going high means the word reads upwards, backwards

parts.note: a pet is a favoured one, as in teacher's pet

explanation.surface: An ancient builder believes the favoured approach is to build tall.
explanation.definitionFit: Imhotep designed the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, the earliest known named architect.

clue.text: Broadcast overlooking Republican's troubled situation

indicators.note: to overlook something is to leave it out, so the Republican's letter is dropped

parts.note: to broadcast seed is to strew or scatter it
R for Republican; the 's joins it to the definition as 'is'

explanation.surface: A broadcast ignores a Republican's political difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' suggests radio or TV, but here it is the farming sense of scattering seed.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a stew is to be in a state of worry or agitation, an idiom for a troubled state.

clue.text: This: really useful supporting structure, primarily

definitions.text: This: really useful supporting structure, primarily

indicators.note: primarily points to the primary, leading letter of each word

parts.note: the five words whose leading letters are taken

explanation.surface: A slogan praising a framework that holds things up.
explanation.definitionFit: A truss is a framework of beams that supports a roof or bridge.

clue.text: Why present for English appears after Welsh

indicators.note: the rest of the word appears after, following on from, the Welsh letter

parts.note: here means present, as at a roll call
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grammar puzzle about why an English word follows a Welsh one.
explanation.definitionFit: Wherefore is an old word for why, as in Juliet's 'wherefore art thou Romeo?'

clue.text: Active karate stars keeping supporting MGM's motto, in other words

indicators.note: the jumbled letters keep the support word inside
active letters are moving about, so these are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to be rearranged
to be for something is to support it

explanation.surface: Busy karate film stars back the studio's famous slogan.
explanation.walkthrough: MGM's lion logo carries the Latin 'Ars gratia artis'; 'in other words' asks for its English version.
explanation.definitionFit: The English phrase translates the Latin Ars gratia artis, the slogan the studio uses.

clue.text: Special type of tie indicating the captain

parts.note: a kipper tie is a very wide necktie fashionable in the 1960s and 70s

explanation.surface: A distinctive necktie marks out the man in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: A kipper is a smoked herring, but a kipper tie is a broad, garish necktie.
explanation.definitionFit: Skipper is an informal title for a ship's master or the leader of a sports team.

clue.text: Sure, this cut, permed, could be shaggy

indicators.note: a perm restyles hair by curling it, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: cut means the word this loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written, then shortened

explanation.surface: A hairdresser says that a particular cut, once permed, might well look shaggy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' and 'permed' both look like hairdressing; one trims a word, the other is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hirsute means hairy, covered with thick unkempt hair, close to shaggy.

clue.text: Crowd accepting feature of Glastonbury — grass — while getting transport in the wet?

indicators.note: the crowd word takes the hill inside it, as if letting it in

parts.note: a mob is a large crowd
Glastonbury Tor is the famous hill above the Somerset town; a tor is a rocky hill
oats are a cereal grass

explanation.surface: Festival-goers at a muddy Glastonbury need a boat to get about in the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: Glastonbury suggests the music festival, but the feature is its landmark hill, Glastonbury Tor.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorboat is a powered vessel, a means of getting about on water, which the question mark jokingly calls 'the wet'.

clue.text: Briefest epithet capturing Shakespearean clown

indicators.note: the two words hold the name within them, catching it across the gap

parts.note: the name runs across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A very short nickname fits one of Shakespeare's comic characters.
explanation.definitionFit: Feste is the fool or jester in Twelfth Night.

clue.text: Early language graduate transcribed in original form

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, a graduate's degree
sic is written after a quotation to show it is copied exactly as the original had it

explanation.surface: A graduate copies out an old language text faithfully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early language' looks like an ancient tongue; it is the 1960s programming language.
explanation.definitionFit: BASIC was one of the first widely used beginner's programming languages, dating from 1964.

clue.text: Sleeping partner to complain loudly about Fed's activity

indicators.note: the bellow word goes about the jumbled letters, around them

parts.note: to bellow is to shout out loud

indicators.note: activity sets the letters in motion, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of Fed; the 's means 'is' in the surface

explanation.surface: A partner moans at the US central bank's doings.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fed is the US Federal Reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedfellow is literally someone you share a bed with, so a sleeping partner.

clue.text: Powerful figure revolutionising our sphere

indicators.note: to revolutionise something is to change it utterly, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A mighty leader transforms the world we live in.
explanation.definitionFit: A superhero is a comic-book character with extraordinary strength or abilities.

clue.text: Place of refuge, over time, upheld in newspaper article

indicators.note: held up in a down entry means the whole is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a lair is an animal's den or hideaway
O for over, the cricket abbreviation
tide is an old word for time, as in Yuletide

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece supports keeping a sanctuary open for a while longer.
explanation.definitionFit: An editorial is a leading article giving a newspaper's own opinion.

clue.text: Nutrition expert to finish with rhino having accepted cases involving one

parts.note: to die is to come to an end

indicators.note: the money word takes the other letters into itself

parts.note: rhino is old British slang for money, as is tin

indicators.note: the cases abbreviation wraps round the one, enclosing it

explanation.surface: A dietary specialist decides to end things with a rhinoceros after taking on some cases.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhino is not an animal but old British slang for cash, like tin.
explanation.definitionFit: A dietician is a professional who advises people on what to eat for health.

clue.text: Cruel and mostly senseless to restrict sound of activity

indicators.note: the shortened word closes around the noise, hemming it in
mostly means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: inane means senseless, silly
the hum of a busy place

explanation.surface: It is cruel and pointless to suppress the noise of busy people.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhuman describes brutal conduct lacking compassion, so it means cruel.

clue.text: Unpleasant rumour about high honour

indicators.note: the rumour word is placed about the honour, around it

parts.note: noise can mean talk or rumour, as in making noises about something
OM, the Order of Merit, a top British honour

explanation.surface: A nasty whisper circulates about someone's elite award.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means offensive or disgusting, especially of a smell, so thoroughly unpleasant.

clue.text: Attention returned when receiving one's extra money

indicators.note: the reversed word takes the other letters inside it
returned means the attention word is read backwards

parts.note: to give someone your ear is to pay attention
I for one, plus 's as is

explanation.surface: Someone gets attention back once their bonus arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: A raise is the American and informal word for a pay increase, more money in the packet.

clue.text: Agricultural threat understood after hesitation

indicators.note: after places the understood word second, following the hesitation

parts.note: er is the sound of someone hesitating
'got it' means understood it

explanation.surface: A farmer hesitates before grasping a danger to the crops.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergot is a fungal disease of rye and other cereals, a serious blight for farmers.

clue.text: Russian writer taking two attempts over line

indicators.note: in a down entry, over means the attempts sit above the line

parts.note: a go is an attempt, so two of them

explanation.surface: A Russian author needs two tries to cross a line.
explanation.definitionFit: Nikolai Gogol was a nineteenth-century novelist and dramatist, author of Dead Souls.

clue.text: Bad weather greets naval fighters around fringes of Tobago

indicators.note: the greeting and the marines sit around the edge letters, enclosing them

parts.note: to hail someone is to greet them
RM, the Royal Marines, the UK's naval infantry

indicators.note: the fringes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: the island name, whose first and last letters are kept

explanation.surface: Stormy weather welcomes a naval force near the coast of a Caribbean island.
explanation.definitionFit: A hailstorm is a storm in which balls of ice fall, an unwelcome kind of weather.

clue.text: Computer peripheral in its thirteenth setting?

parts.note: a mode is a setting on a machine
M is the thirteenth letter, so the thirteenth setting would be mode M

explanation.surface: A puzzled look at a modem buried deep in its menu options.
explanation.walkthrough: If settings were labelled mode A, mode B and so on, the thirteenth would be mode M.
explanation.definitionFit: A modem is a device linking a computer to a telephone or broadband line.

clue.text: Appear to secure — say — third of surplus space

indicators.note: the appearing word holds the other letters fast within it

parts.note: to loom is to appear, often threateningly
eg, for example, is what 'say' means here

indicators.note: the third letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: the word whose third letter is taken

explanation.surface: Someone seems to grab a third of the surplus room for themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Legroom is the room for one's legs, especially in a car, plane or theatre seat.

clue.text: Agreed old reduction in food shortage by date

indicators.note: the shortage word is reduced by losing its last letter

parts.note: a famine is a severe scarcity of food

explanation.surface: An old food crisis eases a little by a certain date, and everyone agrees.
explanation.definitionFit: Being of a mind means sharing the same opinion, in agreement.

clue.text: Pathway regulation overturned by King

indicators.note: a law overturned is reversed, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a law is a regulation

explanation.surface: A rule about a path is struck down by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A walk is a path or promenade laid out for walking.

clue.text: A bullet men forged before the war

indicators.note: forged means hammered into a new shape, so these letters are remade

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Men cast a bullet in the days before conflict began.
explanation.definitionFit: Antebellum is Latin for before the war, used especially of the American South before the Civil War.
